title: Recall Objective Map
user: A self-learner starting a broad topic who needs every review prompt tied to a stated learning objective and visible evidence of what they can actually explain.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker wants learning tools that retain knowledge while tracking what the learner knows and their learning objectives; ChatGPT voice is not set up to do this.
An Anki user asks for a configurable review sidebar that exposes difficulty and stability, showing that existing review metadata is hard to inspect in-context.

recurrence: Two independent 2025–26 learner communities identify the missing layer between a review queue and an intelligible model of progress; it is a recurring setup and motivation failure.
current_workaround: Use an Anki deck beside a separate notes app, or ask a chatbot for ad-hoc questions without a durable objective record.
incumbents_and_gap: Anki/FSRS schedule cards and ChatGPT can converse, but neither makes objective → evidence → weak sub-skill the central, inspectable artifact.
smallest_useful_product: Offline PWA with an objective tree, manual evidence tags (explain, solve, recognize), a one-question recall check, and an exportable weekly weak-skill map. Non-goals: generating course content, a chatbot tutor, or replacing Anki scheduling.
success_measure: In a four-week pilot, 60% of users attach 20+ recall checks to objectives and can name their two weakest objectives without opening a card browser.
monetization: one-time — personal learning records should remain local and useful without a subscription.
constraints: Local-first storage and export; no claims that recall score measures mastery; accessibility for keyboard-only review.
why_distinct: It is an objective/evidence map layered above any study material, not another card scheduler or LLM wrapper.

title: Explain Then Check
user: Technical self-learners who can recognize flashcards but need short, deliberate practice explaining a concept, mechanism, and trade-off in their own words.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A learner of system design and distributed systems asks whether spaced repetition helps with deep understanding; respondents emphasize building and practicing concepts.
A learner describes repeatedly pressing Again without learning the crucial distinction and asks how to avoid brute-force repetition.

recurrence: Independent learners in technical and language domains report the same recognition-versus-understanding gap; the severity is wasted review time and false confidence.
current_workaround: Write free-form notes, explain aloud with no record, make more cards, or rely on a chatbot to ask improvised questions.
incumbents_and_gap: Anki optimizes recall intervals; RemNote and chat tutors collect notes or converse. None makes a 90-second structured explanation with self-selected omissions and later retry the smallest unit.
smallest_useful_product: A local prompt runner: choose a concept, record or type an explanation under headings (what, why, failure case), mark missing pieces, and schedule only those missing pieces for another attempt. Non-goals: answer grading, generated lectures, or shared classrooms.
success_measure: At least half of weekly active users retry five or more marked omissions within seven days, and 70% mark a retry clearer than its first attempt.
monetization: free — a portable practice primitive benefits from frictionless adoption and plaintext export.
constraints: Audio remains on device by default; no automated claim that an explanation is correct; support export/delete.
why_distinct: It trains generative explanation without pretending an LLM can certify understanding.

title: Source-to-Recall Gate
user: Students converting highlights into study prompts who need to decide what is worth remembering and encode it as a personally meaningful recall cue before it becomes queue debt.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The discussion distinguishes spaced repetition as retrieval from the separate encoding work required to make knowledge one's own.
A reader who forgets books wants to import highlights but explicitly does not want to memorize paragraphs, exposing the highlight-to-recall design problem.

recurrence: Both threads describe adding material before deciding what the learner can retrieve from it; this routinely produces bloated decks and abandoned review habits.
current_workaround: Dump highlights into Readwise/Notion, import cloze deletions wholesale, or reread passages on a schedule.
incumbents_and_gap: Readwise captures highlights and Anki reviews finished cards; neither imposes a tiny decision gate: why this matters, what cue will retrieve it, and what concrete example proves it.
smallest_useful_product: Browser extension and PWA that saves a selected passage locally, requires one paraphrase, one cue, and one use-case before export as Markdown/CSV/Anki TSV. Non-goals: web scraping, AI-generated cards, cloud highlight sync, or a reader app.
success_measure: In a 30-day cohort, users export fewer than 50% of captured highlights but review 70%+ of those exports at least twice.
monetization: one-time — a local export utility has a clear individual value and no server cost.
constraints: Only user-selected text; no copying of protected books into a service; local storage, clipboard permissions, and clear data deletion.
why_distinct: It deliberately reduces card creation and makes encoding quality visible instead of automating more flashcards.

title: Concept Case Bridge
user: Professionals learning both a technical stack and an unfamiliar business domain who need to practice choosing the right concept in a realistic domain case.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker says business-domain knowledge is as difficult as technical knowledge, while most learning tools focus only on the technical stack.
An add-on was built because recognizing vocabulary or facts on a card is different from understanding them in a paragraph; it filters forgotten or vague items into context.

recurrence: The same transfer gap appears across professional and card-review contexts: isolated facts are retained, but application in context is not.
current_workaround: Keep separate domain notes, wait for real work exposure, or ask an LLM to invent examples that are difficult to trust or revisit.
incumbents_and_gap: Anki, Obsidian, and generated-reading add-ons store facts or create prose; they do not maintain a reusable, authored link from concept to domain signal, decision, and counterexample.
smallest_useful_product: Local case-card editor: author a compact scenario, tag the technical concept and domain signal, hide the decision, and review with a 'why not the alternative?' field. Non-goals: domain-content marketplace, automatic case generation, or certification testing.
success_measure: Pilot users create 15+ concept-case links and correctly choose the intended concept in 75% of delayed case checks after two weeks.
monetization: one-time — private professional context is sensitive and does not need hosted accounts.
constraints: Do not include employer-confidential facts in templates; local-only default; authored cases need clear attribution/export.
why_distinct: The atomic unit is a transfer decision with a counterexample, not a flashcard or generated reading passage.

title: Audio Reflection Markers
user: Podcast and lecture listeners who need to turn a personally useful moment into one short recall/action prompt without trying to summarize an entire episode.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker says podcast insights are passively consumed and not retained or applied; commenters describe highlights flowing into a separate system.
A language learner wants to create cards while watching, with screenshots, rather than export subtitles and move between several tools.

recurrence: Two media-learning workflows expose capture fragmentation: the useful moment passes while the listener is forced into transcription, export, and later card creation.
current_workaround: Bookmark timestamps, make voice notes, use Snipd/Readwise, or manually create a document of Q&A later.
incumbents_and_gap: Podcast apps bookmark and Readwise stores highlights, but neither has a deliberately small 'timestamp + my takeaway + next retrieval cue' flow that is format-agnostic and export-first.
smallest_useful_product: Mobile-first PWA for user-supplied audio/video links or local files: one-button timestamp marker, typed/voice takeaway, optional action date, and Markdown/CSV export. Non-goals: downloading platforms' media, automatic episode transcription, summaries, or public clip sharing.
success_measure: In four weeks, 50% of saved markers receive a follow-up recall/action check, with median capture time under 20 seconds.
monetization: free — no hosted media processing keeps the privacy and copyright model straightforward.
constraints: Use only local files or user-entered timestamps/links; do not fetch or redistribute copyrighted audio; microphone permission is optional and local.
why_distinct: It captures an intentional learning commitment, not a transcript, AI summary, or media library.

title: Minimal Pair Recorder
user: Independent language learners and mobile-first teachers who need repeatable listening-and-speaking drills for easily confused sounds without depending on a generative tutor.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A learner explicitly asks for interactive language-learning tools that do not use LLMs/GenAI.
A teacher with 1,000+ sentence cards says robotic Android TTS is inadequate where pronunciation precision matters and PC-only add-ons are unavailable.

recurrence: A demand for non-GenAI interaction and a teacher's mobile pronunciation constraint converge on a small, offline-capable drill rather than another general language course.
current_workaround: Replay unreliable TTS, use desktop-only add-ons, record isolated voice notes, or use broad apps whose pronunciation exercises cannot target a teacher's exact pairs.
incumbents_and_gap: Duolingo and speech-recognition apps are broad curricula; Anki stores audio but does not offer a focused, shareable minimal-pair listen/record/contrast loop.
smallest_useful_product: Offline PWA where a teacher imports or records two short reference sounds, publishes a QR drill, and learners choose, record, replay, and self-compare. Non-goals: automatic accent scoring, cloud TTS, a language curriculum, or learner surveillance.
success_measure: In a pilot class, 70% of learners complete three recorded contrast attempts per assigned pair and improve blind pair-identification accuracy by 20 percentage points.
monetization: one-time — teacher-created offline drill packs should work in low-connectivity settings.
constraints: Get consent before storing/sharing recordings; use teacher-owned or public-domain reference audio; never claim clinical pronunciation assessment.
why_distinct: It is a privacy-preserving contrast practice tool, not an AI conversational language tutor.

title: Rubric Revision Loop
user: Teachers with a large writing-feedback load who need to give reusable, criterion-specific feedback and make the student's next revision visible without outsourcing judgment to an LLM.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A current teacher discussion asks how writing feedback can be handled at scale; the visible response reports doing it manually.
A learner asks for simple, shareable, non-breaking content templates and explicitly finds existing options too complicated to modify.

recurrence: The direct feedback-scale question plus demand for simple shareable learning templates points to teacher workflows breaking when every learner artifact needs custom technical setup.
current_workaround: Write repeated comments in Docs/LMS, use generic comment banks, or accept AI feedback that is hard to calibrate and explain.
incumbents_and_gap: Google Classroom, Canvas, and Turnitin collect comments; generative writing tools produce text. The gap is a lightweight loop that connects a human rubric code to the student's concrete revision evidence.
smallest_useful_product: Teacher-created rubric-code library, pasteable short feedback links, student revision checklist with before/after excerpt, and teacher review queue. Non-goals: essay generation, plagiarism detection, grading automation, or LMS replacement.
success_measure: A teacher reuses rubric codes for 50%+ of comments while 60%+ of students submit at least one linked revision explanation.
monetization: freemium — a free single-class workflow validates utility; small paid teams need shared rubrics and retention controls.
constraints: Student data minimization, FERPA/GDPR-aware deletion, no model training on student writing, accessible link-only student view.
why_distinct: It scales a teacher's reasons and revision dialogue rather than producing synthetic feedback or acting as an LMS.

title: Tutor Session Trace
user: One-to-one remote coding tutors who need a lightweight record of student attempts, handoffs, and next practice tasks while teaching through existing video and editor tools.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A teacher/tutor asks what is frustrating about remote coding lessons and lists the fragmented Zoom, Replit, and VS Code Live Share stack.
A Live Share outage report has 132 reactions, underscoring that the collaboration layer itself is not a dependable place to keep lesson context.

recurrence: Tutors describe multi-tool instruction while a highly reacted collaboration outage demonstrates the operational fragility of putting the whole lesson inside a shared editor session.
current_workaround: Keep notes in a separate document, send chat follow-ups, record a video, or rely on the editor's transient session state.
incumbents_and_gap: Zoom, Replit, and Live Share provide communication/co-editing but not a tutor-owned attempt timeline with explicit next practice and no repository access requirement.
smallest_useful_product: A small web app with timestamped lesson moments, attempt/outcome tags, code snippet or link attachment, student-visible next task, and PDF/Markdown recap. Non-goals: video calling, code execution, proctoring, or a full LMS.
success_measure: After ten sessions, 80% of recaps are opened by the student and tutors create a next-practice item in at least 70% of sessions.
monetization: freemium — solo tutors can use a limited free log; client history and exports justify a modest paid tier.
constraints: Avoid storing credentials or full private repositories; explicit student consent for notes; configurable deletion and share expiry.
why_distinct: It preserves the pedagogical trace around an existing coding session rather than competing with editors or video calls.

title: Vocab Confusion Log
user: Language learners who repeatedly confuse near-neighbor words or spellings and need a short contrast-and-production repair, not another generic review interval.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker says vocabulary does not stick long-term despite streaks and flashcards, and asks which features improve durable recall.
A Japanese learner needs parallel text-reading and audio-only prompts but cannot duplicate the workflow without losing progress and course pacing.

recurrence: Users report that a single card mode does not repair a durable vocabulary failure; a second retrieval modality is needed without duplicating a whole deck.
current_workaround: Press Again repeatedly, make duplicate cards/decks, attach mnemonic notes, or drill an entire vocabulary list again.
incumbents_and_gap: Anki supports custom cards and Duolingo supplies exercises, but neither presents a compact confusion record: wrong answer, intended word, contrast cue, audio/text retry, and resolution history.
smallest_useful_product: Local PWA to log one confused pair, attach text/audio/own mnemonic, rotate text-to-audio and audio-to-text retries, and export resolved pairs as CSV. Non-goals: language content marketplace, speech scoring, or full SRS scheduling.
success_measure: Users resolve 50% of logged pairs (three clean delayed attempts) within 21 days, with fewer than one new duplicate deck per active user.
monetization: one-time — the data is personal and the narrowly useful workflow needs no recurring service.
constraints: Local recordings by default; teacher/imported audio needs rights; no unsupported claim of language proficiency measurement.
why_distinct: It targets the error pattern that generic flashcard schedules hide, rather than adding more cards or gamification.

title: Review Backlog Restart
user: Spaced-repetition users returning after a break who need an honest, manageable restart plan that protects high-risk material without forcing an all-night catch-up session.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An Ask HN user questions why a flashcard app makes the learner self-rate recall, highlighting the uncertainty and burden placed on the user during review.
After a two-week break, a language learner has 400 due cards and faces either a huge sitting or a reset; their one-day cards will otherwise return about a month late.

recurrence: One thread challenges subjective review control and another shows a concrete 500-card failure mode; the consequence is users abandoning otherwise valuable study history.
current_workaround: Set arbitrary daily limits, reset cards, grind through the queue, or abandon the deck and start again.
incumbents_and_gap: Anki exposes scheduler settings and FSRS estimates retention, but returning learners lack a simple what-to-do-next plan that makes the workload/retention tradeoff explicit.
smallest_useful_product: Local companion that imports an Anki CSV export, asks for daily minutes and deadline, simulates three recovery plans, flags highest-risk cards, and exports a tagged action list. Non-goals: syncing to Anki, replacing FSRS, or making retention guarantees.
success_measure: At least 50% of users with a 100+ card backlog follow a plan for seven days and reduce due cards by 30% without resetting the collection.
monetization: free — recovery needs to be available at the moment a learner is most likely to quit.
constraints: Read-only imports; do not alter scheduling data; clearly label projections as estimates and keep all study history local.
why_distinct: It is a recovery decision aid, not a scheduler, deck, or generic productivity timer.

title: Prerequisite Sprint Map
user: A learner beginning a technical subject who needs to identify the smallest prerequisite set, practice it, and start the target topic rather than stall in an endless prerequisite search.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A learner asks which maths is required before data structures; a response advises not waiting and suggests discrete maths before or alongside the target subject.
The author calls deadline-based review planning one of the most commonly requested scheduling features and links many independent student requests for an exam date.

recurrence: Prerequisite uncertainty and deadline pressure create the same damaging behavior: learners defer the real subject while making an unbounded study plan.
current_workaround: Search Reddit/course syllabi, construct a large Notion plan, collect resources, or choose a generic curriculum with no concrete start criterion.
incumbents_and_gap: Roadmap sites and course platforms show broad curricula; Anki schedules review. Neither gives a learner a bounded prerequisite contract plus a date-aware 'start target material now' checkpoint.
smallest_useful_product: Static web/PWA planner with editable prerequisite nodes, a diagnostic checkbox per node, target-date capacity math, and a visible start-now lane alongside prerequisite work. Non-goals: adaptive testing, hosting courses, content generation, or credential advice.
success_measure: In a two-week test, 65% of users complete a target-topic exercise before completing every optional prerequisite node.
monetization: free — shareable subject templates are more valuable as an open, editable reference.
constraints: State assumptions per template; avoid representing a path as universally sufficient; no collection of minors' educational data.
why_distinct: It helps learners escape prerequisite paralysis with bounded decisions, not by selling another course catalogue.

title: Claim Source Trail
user: Undergraduate humanities and social-science students learning digital research workflows who need to practice attaching a claim to an exact source location and a reason it supports the claim.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An instructor asks how to teach digital research workflows to undergraduate philosophy students, specifically seeking open, open-access, free tools and presentation guidance.
A Zotero issue requests page-number suggestions in the citation dialog for open documents, showing that even citation tooling lacks a smooth exact-location handoff.

recurrence: Teaching digital research is explicitly current, while a current citation-tool request shows the practical friction at the source-location step where student evidence trails often fail.
current_workaround: Keep a document of copied quotes, use Zotero notes with loose annotations, or add citations only when drafting the final essay.
incumbents_and_gap: Zotero manages references and Google Docs formats citations; neither teaches or validates the small reasoning chain claim → exact locator → paraphrase → why it supports the claim.
smallest_useful_product: Privacy-first web app with a four-field claim card, DOI/URL/author citation metadata, page/section locator, counterevidence flag, and export to Markdown/CSV. Non-goals: scraping paywalled sources, automatic fact checking, essay generation, or a reference manager replacement.
success_measure: In one classroom pilot, 75% of submitted claims include a verifiable locator and instructor spot checks find fewer than 10% unsupported claim-source links.
monetization: freemium — a free private student tier supports adoption; instructor cohorts and retention controls can fund hosted use.
constraints: Store citations and learner notes only with clear deletion; respect publisher access/copyright; avoid claims of truth verification; WCAG-friendly keyboard workflow.
why_distinct: It teaches evidentiary reasoning at the claim level instead of becoming an AI essay writer or another bibliography manager.
